personas.name: Sam
personas.profile: Sam, 34, a freelance developer who keeps about a dozen of their own repos green on GitHub Actions. They run the flakeslash CLI on a laptop at the weekend and want to know which test to fix first before they touch anything.

focus.dashboard: whether the catalogue shows which flake to fix first, whether the issue page shows the commit where it started, and whether a quick look needs no sign-in step.
focus.report: whether report.html opens at once on a laptop without a server, whether the top flakes are the ones worth an afternoon this week, and whether each one says what to change.
focus.cli: whether the output says in plain words which tests flake and how often, whether the exit codes (0, 1, 2) are what a shell script needs, and whether a usage mistake gets a clear message and exit 2.

personas.name: Dana
personas.profile: Dana, 41, engineering lead of a team of about ten. She installed the GitHub App for the whole organisation and wants to know which flakes cost the team the most time, and whether a fix is worth the cost of the work.

focus.dashboard: whether the catalogue order matches what hurts the team most, whether teams and CODEOWNERS owners are visible on each issue, and whether the reliability overview shows a trend she could show her manager.
focus.report: whether the report ranks flakes by CI minutes lost and by commits affected in the last 30 days, whether each flake names an owner, and whether the numbers are clear enough to paste into a planning document.
focus.cli: whether the summary gives minutes lost and flake counts by repo, whether the output is stable enough for a shared CI job to read, and whether a failed run says whether the cause is the tool or the token.

personas.name: Marcus
personas.profile: Marcus, 38, maintains a popular open-source library. Outside contributors keep opening pull requests that go red on CI for reasons that are not their fault, and he answers the same question about flaky tests every week.

focus.dashboard: whether a PR page says already flaking on main clearly enough for a contributor to read it without help, and whether the public view shows only what a viewer is allowed to see.
focus.report: whether the report separates a flake in the code from one in the runner, so he can tell a contributor it is not their change, and whether each entry links back to the failing job.
focus.cli: whether a contributor can run the CLI on a public repo with a token that has no more rights than it needs, and whether the output names the test well enough to paste into an issue.

personas.name: Ines
personas.profile: Ines, 45, a platform engineer at a mid-size company that runs its own CI runners. She is weighing whether to self-host FlakeSlash on the company's infrastructure, and she reads the data-retention and deployment story before anything else.

focus.dashboard: whether the self-hosted setup and the data retention are plain (detailed rows for 90 days, flake records kept), whether the runner and provider breakdown is shown, and whether sign-in and the GitHub App look safe for a company to approve.
focus.report: whether the report says which runner a flake came from (GitHub-hosted, Depot, Blacksmith or self-hosted), so a runner fault shows up as a runner fault, and whether it keeps only redacted excerpts.
focus.cli: whether the scan can be pointed at her own server with a clear flag, whether an unreachable server ends in exit 1 with a message she can act on, and whether the output says what was sent and what was kept.

personas.name: The tools designer
personas.profile: An experienced developer-tools designer who has shipped command-line tools and dashboards that engineers use every day. Judges the craft of what the product shows, not whether the product is needed.

focus.dashboard: the information hierarchy of the catalogue and issue pages, whether rank and status read without colour, whether the light and dark themes feel like one design, and whether the page looks like a template or something made for this job.
focus.report: the hierarchy, contrast and legibility of the report, whether the tables line up and the numbers carry clear units, and whether it looks like a template or something made for this job.
focus.cli: whether the output is scannable at a glance, whether spacing, alignment and wording are consistent, whether an error says what to do next, and whether colour is used with restraint and the output still reads without it.
